title: Homemade White Pudding with Turkey and Beef Suet
excerpt: This turkey-and-oat white pudding uses finely chopped beef suet, onion and warm spices for a savory breakfast pudding. Fill beef casings, gently poach the links, then chill and pan-fry thick slices until golden. Plan ahead for the chilling time and serve with eggs, tomatoes or toast.
featuredImageAlt: Golden pan-fried white pudding rounds with a savory oat filling
contentHtml:
This turkey-and-oat white pudding uses finely chopped beef suet, onion and warm spices for a savory breakfast pudding. Fill beef casings, gently poach the links, then chill and pan-fry thick slices until golden. Plan ahead for the chilling time and serve with eggs, tomatoes or toast.

This is a turkey-and-oat adaptation of white pudding, with beef suet providing richness and beef casings holding the mixture together during poaching. The seasoning stays simple: onion, white pepper, nutmeg and a little sage.

  • Kitchen scale and measuring jugFor weighing the oats, meat and suet and measuring the broth.
  • Large mixing bowlFor hydrating the oats and mixing the chilled filling.
  • Sausage stuffer or filling funnelFor loosely filling prepared beef casings; use a suitable nozzle.
  • Large poaching potLarge enough for the links to sit below the water without crowding.
  • Food thermometerFor checking the centers of the links and reheated slices.
  • Shallow container and skilletFor chilling the cooked pudding and frying the sliced rounds.

Why You’ll Love This White Pudding

  • The beef suet and chilled turkey give the oat filling richness and structure.
  • Poaching first and chilling thoroughly help the slices hold together in the pan.
  • You can prepare the links the day before and fry the slices for breakfast.
  • Simple spices let the oats, onion and turkey remain the focus.

Ingredients

Keep the turkey and finely chopped beef suet cold until mixing. Use beef casings that are labeled for cooking, and prepare them according to the package.

  • 200 g rolled oats (use regular rolled oats, not steel-cut oats)
  • 300 ml cold unsalted turkey or chicken broth
  • 400 g ground turkey, chilled
  • 100 g fresh beef suet, finely chopped and chilled
  • 1 medium onion, about 150 g, very finely chopped
  • 50 g plain breadcrumbs
  • 1 teaspoon fine salt
  • 1/2 teaspoon ground white pepper
  • 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg
  • 1/2 teaspoon dried sage
  • Food-grade beef sausage casings, about 35–40 mm diameter, prepared according to the package
  • 2 teaspoons neutral oil, for pan-frying the slices

How to Make White Pudding with Turkey

Allow about 20 minutes of preparation, 30 minutes for the oats to hydrate, roughly 55 minutes of cooking and at least 4 hours of chilling, plus a short initial cooling period. Cooking time depends on the diameter of the links.

Step 1: Hydrate the Oats

Combine the rolled oats and cold broth in a bowl. Cover and refrigerate for 30 minutes so the oats soften. Prepare the beef casings according to their package directions while keeping the turkey and suet chilled.

Step 2: Mix the Turkey Filling

Mix the cold ground turkey with the salt, white pepper, nutmeg and sage until slightly tacky. Fold in the hydrated oats with their liquid, finely chopped beef suet, onion and breadcrumbs. The mixture should be moist and spoonable, not runny; if unusually dry, add a little extra cold broth a tablespoon at a time.

Step 3: Fill the Beef Casings

Using a clean sausage stuffer or filling funnel, fill the prepared beef casings loosely. Leave room for expansion, work out large air pockets, and tie manageable links that fit your poaching pot. Keep the filled links refrigerated until the water is ready.

Step 4: Prepare the Poaching Water

Heat a large pot of water to about 180°F (82°C). Lower in the links gently, working in batches if necessary. Keep the water hot with only an occasional bubble rather than a rolling boil.

Step 5: Poach to 165°F

Poach for about 45 minutes, beginning temperature checks after 35 minutes. Insert a food thermometer into the center of the thickest links and continue cooking until they reach at least 165°F (74°C). Link size changes the cooking time, so use the temperature rather than the clock to judge doneness.

Step 6: Cool and Chill

Lift the cooked links onto a clean tray and cool briefly, about 15 minutes; an ice bath can help cool them promptly. Transfer to a shallow covered container in the refrigerator and chill for at least 4 hours, or overnight, until firm enough to slice. Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking.

Step 7: Slice and Pan-Fry

Cut the chilled pudding into rounds about 1 cm thick. Heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat and fry the slices in batches for about 2–3 minutes per side, until golden and the centers reach 165°F (74°C). Use a little longer if necessary.

Step 8: Serve

Serve hot with eggs, grilled tomatoes, sautéed mushrooms or toast. Keep unused pudding refrigerated and use within 3–4 days of the original cooking date, or freeze for longer storage.

The USDA sausage cooking guidance specifies 165°F for sausages containing ground turkey or chicken.

Pro Tips for Making White Pudding

  • Chop the cold beef suet finely so it distributes through the filling.
  • Keep the filling chilled while preparing the casings and poaching water.
  • Fill loosely and leave room for expansion; packed-tight casings can split.
  • Keep the poaching water below a rolling boil and use a thermometer for doneness.
  • Chill thoroughly before slicing. Thin or warm slices are more likely to crumble.
  • Cook a small test portion fully before tasting and adjusting the seasoning; never taste raw turkey filling.

How to Serve White Pudding

  • Serve hot slices with eggs and buttered toast.
  • Add grilled tomatoes, sautéed mushrooms or wilted greens.
  • Tuck a few slices into a breakfast roll with a spoonful of tomato relish.

Make Ahead and Storage

Refrigerating

Refrigerate the cooked pudding promptly in shallow covered containers, within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour in temperatures above 90°F (32°C). Keep the refrigerator at 40°F (4°C) or below. Use within 3–4 days of the original cooking date, including any overnight chilling time.

Freezing

Freeze cooked, cooled links or slices in airtight portions for up to 2 months for best quality. Label with the cooking date and thaw in the refrigerator.

Reheating

Pan-fry thawed or refrigerated slices in a little oil until golden and the centers reach 165°F (74°C). Reheat only the portion you plan to eat.

For cooked meat and poultry storage, see the USDA refrigeration guidance.

FAQs

What replaces the original suet?

Finely chopped beef suet provides the fat in this version. The filling also contains ground turkey, oats, onion and spices, and the links use beef casings.

Which oats should I use?

Use regular rolled oats for the 30-minute hydration step. Steel-cut oats need a different soaking and cooking schedule, so they are not a direct swap here.

Do I need a sausage stuffer?

A sausage stuffer is helpful, especially for repeated batches, but a suitable filling funnel can also fill the beef casings. Prepare the casings and choose a nozzle according to the equipment and casing instructions.

Can I make white pudding ahead of time?

Yes. Poach the links, cool them promptly and refrigerate in a shallow covered container. Chilling overnight makes slicing easier. Count the 3–4-day refrigerated storage period from the day the pudding was first cooked.

How do I know the turkey filling is cooked?

Check the center of the thickest links with a food thermometer. Ground turkey needs to reach 165°F (74°C); the estimated poaching time alone does not establish doneness.

Can I freeze the cooked pudding?

Freeze cooled links or slices in airtight portions for up to 2 months for best quality. Thaw in the refrigerator, then reheat slices to 165°F (74°C).

Bring It to the Breakfast Table

Make the links ahead, give them time to chill, then fry a few slices when you are ready to serve. The result is a hearty turkey-and-oat breakfast pudding with a golden outside and a savory center.
